topics.title: Croatia Citizenship Requirements
topics.summary: Croatia's ordinary naturalisation route combines eight continuous years of registered residence with permanent status, language and civic knowledge, and normally release from previous citizenship.
topics.scope: Selected adult ordinary naturalisation requirements under Article 8, checked against current Ministry guidance and the operative amendments; facilitated family, descent and national-interest routes are separate.

facts.label: Eight continuous years and permanent status
facts.text: An ordinary applicant must be at least 18, have lived in Croatia with registered residence continuously for eight years up to application, and hold approved permanent-resident status. Eight years of merely owning property or visiting does not satisfy that requirement.
facts.locator: Ministry FAQ: naturalisation; 2011 amendment Article 2 replacing Act Article 8(1)(3); 2019 amendment Article 3

constraint.cohort: Ordinary Article 8 applicant: continuous registered residence through application, with approved permanent status also required

facts.label: Release requirement has defined exceptions
facts.text: Ordinarily provide release from the existing citizenship or proof that release will follow admission. Statelessness or automatic loss can satisfy this condition. If release is unavailable or subject to impossible conditions, a conditional renunciation statement is accepted under the Ministry's stated exception.
facts.locator: FAQ: whether release from foreign citizenship is required, Article 8(1)(2) and associated exceptions

facts.label: Several Croatian-language proof routes
facts.text: Accepted evidence includes an authorised examination, completed Croatian primary, secondary or higher education, or qualifying foreign higher-education documentation at least at B1. B1 belongs to that last proof route, not a universal numerical level established for every applicant. Special refugee and returnee cohorts have separate proof arrangements.
facts.locator: Regulation Articles 2-3: accepted language/Latin-script evidence and limited alternative proof cohorts

facts.label: Culture test and over-60 exemption
facts.text: The culture and social-order questionnaire has 15 questions, with at least 10 correct answers required. Applicants over 60 are exempt from the language, Latin-script, culture and social-order knowledge conditions; this is not an exemption from the other naturalisation requirements.
facts.locator: Regulation Articles 5-6; Ministry FAQ on age; 2011 amendment Article 2 introducing Act Article 8(5)

facts.label: Legal compliance and public dues
facts.text: The applicant must demonstrate respect for Croatia's legal order, payment of due public charges and absence of security impediments. Residence and language evidence alone therefore do not establish eligibility.
facts.locator: 2019 amendment Article 3 replacing Act Article 8(1)(5); current naturalisation FAQ

facts.label: Personal application and supporting documents
facts.text: Applications are normally filed personally with the police authority responsible for the applicant's residence. A representative may act for an applicant with a disability. Identification, civil-status and criminal-record evidence are among the required documents; the residence period is not a promised processing time.
facts.locator: Submitting an application and documents to submit with the application

limits: Marriage to a Croatian citizen, qualifying life partnerships, emigrants and descendants, former citizens and national-interest grants have separate conditions; the ordinary eight-year rule is not a universal waiting period.
The sources do not establish a universal CEFR level for ordinary naturalisation. Do not convert the culture test or the over-60 exemption into a CEFR score.
Permission to acquire or retain other citizenships must also be checked under the other country's law. This is not a complete document checklist or a guarantee of admission.

topics.title: Croatia Tax Residence and Foreign Income
topics.summary: Croatian tax residence can arise from an available home or habitual abode, not only days physically spent there. Residents generally face worldwide income taxation, subject to applicable exemptions and treaties.
topics.scope: Selected individual income-tax residence, taxable-scope and residence-change rules; not a calculation of local rates, social contributions, business taxes or a person's treaty outcome.

facts.label: Resident worldwide scope; non-resident sources
facts.text: Residents generally have Croatian domicile or habitual abode and are taxed on domestic and foreign income in the listed taxable categories. Non-residents generally face Croatian-source income tax. Croatian state-service employees paid for that service abroad can also be resident despite having neither domestic domicile nor habitual abode.
facts.locator: Porezni obveznik and Porezna osnovica: residents, non-residents and taxable income categories

facts.label: A home test is not a physical-day test
facts.text: Tax domicile can exist where a dwelling is owned or possessed continuously for at least 183 days across one or two calendar years. Actual residence in that dwelling is not required. Family, usual residence and work-departure ties help decide between multiple homes.
facts.locator: Opening General Tax Act domicile explanation and multiple-home rules

facts.label: Habitual abode uses connected presence
facts.text: Habitual abode requires circumstances showing more than a temporary stay. The rule counts a continuous or connected stay of at least 183 days across one or two calendar years; temporary interruptions of no more than one year are disregarded.
facts.locator: Uobičajeno boravište paragraph: duration and temporary interruptions

facts.label: Competing residence claims need a treaty check
facts.text: An applicable tax treaty can resolve competing residence claims. The Administration explains the usual sequence of permanent home, vital interests, habitual abode, nationality and authority agreement. The actual treaty and the person's facts control; a Croatian passport alone is not the residence test.
facts.locator: Explanation of Article 4 OECD-model treaty residence tie-breaks

facts.label: Residence changes require evidence
facts.text: The Administration uses questionnaire TU for non-resident-to-resident changes and TI for resident-to-non-resident changes, supported by relevant evidence. Moving abroad or changing an address should not be treated as an automatic tax clearance.
facts.locator: Questionnaires TU and TI and supporting residence evidence

limits: Taxable categories, statutory exemptions and treaty relief still matter within worldwide scope. Local income-tax rates, payroll withholding, social insurance and special regimes are not covered here.
The domicile and habitual-abode rules differ from immigration residence. No generic rule that fewer than 183 physical days makes a person non-resident is supported.

topics.title: Romania Citizenship Requirements
topics.summary: Romania's ordinary naturalisation rules require qualifying residence and a settled residence right, means and good conduct, plus an interview assessing Romanian language and civic knowledge.
topics.scope: Selected adult Article 8 ordinary naturalisation rules as amended from 15 March 2025. Earlier pending applications retain the substantive eligibility rules applicable when filed; restoration and descent under Articles 10-11 are separate.

facts.label: Eight years plus a settled residence right
facts.text: An applicant aged at least 18 must hold long-term or permanent residence rights when applying and have at least eight years of lawful residence. The married route instead requires at least five years of lawful residence since marriage while married to and living with a Romanian citizen, still with the required residence rights.
facts.locator: Law 14/2025 Article I point 3 replacing Act Article 8(1)(a), (c); Article XIV transitional rule

constraint.cohort: Ordinary Article 8 application under the post-15-March-2025 rule, also requiring long-term or permanent residence rights at filing; married and reduced-period cohorts are separate

facts.label: Absences and reductions are qualified
facts.text: An absence exceeding six months in a year excludes that year. The eight-year period can be reduced by up to three years for qualifying EU/EEA/Swiss or Romania-born applicants only with the statutory participation or contribution conditions; recognised refugees need the separate exceptional-integration assessment. These are not automatic nationality discounts.
facts.locator: Law 14/2025 Article I point 3: replacement Article 8(2)-(4), including qualifying birth and integration conditions

facts.label: Means, loyalty and good conduct
facts.text: Applicants must show lawful means for a decent living, loyalty to the Romanian state and constitutional values, and good conduct. Conduct or convictions incompatible with citizenship, undermining the legal order or national-security concerns can prevent admission.
facts.locator: Law 14/2025 Article I point 3 replacing Act Article 8(1)(b), (d)-(e)

facts.label: Romanian language and civic interview
facts.text: The ordinary interview assesses reading, writing and oral Romanian alongside history, geography, culture, the Constitution and anthem. A mean mark of at least 5 out of 10 is required. The procedure provides disability adaptations; applicants under the specified court protective measures are exempt from the interview.
facts.locator: Procedure sections 2, 3.1.3-3.1.4, 3.3.2 and 3.4.1-3.4.9

facts.label: Ordinary-route CEFR level not established
facts.text: The reviewed Article 8 interview rules do not establish a general CEFR level. The B1 certificate provisions for Article 10 or 11 restoration and descendant applications must not be presented as the universal ordinary-naturalisation requirement.
facts.locator: Law 14/2025 Article I points 3 and 16: Act Article 8(1)(f)-(g) versus Article 15^1(4); interview procedure without CEFR mapping

facts.label: No Article 8 renunciation condition; oath matters
facts.text: Article 8 does not list surrendering another citizenship as an admission condition. Another country's law may nevertheless remove that nationality. Meeting the Romanian conditions does not create an automatic entitlement; citizenship is normally acquired on taking the allegiance oath after approval.
facts.locator: Law 14/2025 Article I points 1, 3, 8, 22-23 replacing Act Articles 4(2), 8, 12 and 20(1), subject to the exceptional Article 21 arrangements

limits: For the Romania-born reduced-period cohort, at least one parent must have been lawfully resident when the applicant was born. Reduction also requires the specified active economic participation, relevant educational achievement or exceptional contribution; it is not available merely because a person was born in Romania.

The 2025 substantive rules are not retroactively imposed on every pending application. Law 14/2025 Article XIV preserves the filing-date eligibility rules for earlier pending cases; procedural provisions have their own transition rules.

No processing-time promise, universal B1 rule or restoration-by-descent entitlement is inferred. Future electronic-filing provisions and the 2026 certificate-deadline changes for Articles 10-11 are not ordinary-route eligibility changes.

topics.title: Romania Tax Residence and Foreign Income
topics.summary: Romanian tax residence depends on domicile, vital interests or qualifying presence. Worldwide scope has foreign-employment and treaty qualifications, and moving to a non-treaty country can preserve a longer tax obligation.
topics.scope: Selected individual residence and taxable-income scope under ANAF's Fiscal Code updated through Emergency Ordinance 38/2026, with its stated 2025 residence guide; not personal tax advice or a tax-rate comparison.

facts.label: Alternative residence tests
facts.text: Domestic residence tests include Romanian domicile, a Romanian centre of vital interests, or presence exceeding 183 days in any consecutive twelve-month period ending in the calendar year concerned. Romanian citizens serving abroad as officials or employees of the Romanian state have a separate rule, not applicable to all citizens abroad.
facts.locator: Article 7 point 28(a)-(d)

facts.label: Worldwide versus Romanian-source income
facts.text: Residents generally enter worldwide taxation for taxable income categories, while non-residents face the specified Romanian-source obligations. For the presence trigger, worldwide scope starts from the first arrival day; for vital interests, from the first day declared as such. Treaty residence and statutory exemptions can change the result.
facts.locator: Article 59(1)-(3); residence guide section 3.2.4, printed page 6

facts.label: Foreign employment has a specific exclusion
facts.text: Employment abroad paid by a non-resident employer is generally not taxable or reportable in Romania. Pay by or on behalf of an employer resident in Romania or having a Romanian permanent establishment is different where Romania has the taxing right. This is not an all-foreign-income exemption.
facts.locator: Article 76(4)(o) and methodological rule 19 concerning work performed abroad

facts.label: A non-treaty move can leave a tax tail
facts.text: A Romanian-resident individual domiciled in Romania who proves a move to a non-treaty country remains within worldwide scope for the change year and the next three calendar years. A treaty-country move instead needs evidence establishing the residence-change date under that treaty.
facts.locator: Residence guide section 4.1, printed page 9; Article 59(5)-(7)

facts.label: Arrival and departure questionnaires
facts.text: Qualifying arrivals exceeding 183 days file the residence questionnaire within 30 days after that threshold. Covered departures exceeding 183 days abroad in twelve months require a questionnaire 30 days before leaving. Foreign residence certificates and supporting evidence matter; diplomatic and state-service exceptions must be checked separately.
facts.locator: Sections 3.2.1-3.2.3 and 3.3.2-3.3.4, printed pages 4-5 and 7-8

facts.label: Treaty credit or exemption is conditional
facts.text: Applicable treaties can provide foreign-tax credit or exemption. Credit requires supporting proof and is capped by the Romanian tax attributable to that foreign income, calculated separately by source country and income category.
facts.locator: Article 131: foreign-tax credit and exemption conditions

limits: Romanian nationality alone does not establish worldwide taxation. Domicile, residence-change dates, the particular income and the applicable treaty require separate assessment.

The special foreign-employment exclusion is not a general exemption for pensions, rent, dividends, self-employment or investment income. Rates, withholding, social contributions and detailed return calculations are outside this baseline.

ANAF labels the online Code a computer-generated consolidation rather than an official republication. The guide file name contains 2023, but the actual document is the 2025 edition; it is not described here as a new 2026 publication.

topics.title: Bulgaria Citizenship Requirements
topics.summary: Bulgaria's ordinary naturalisation clock starts with permanent or long-term residence permission. Language evidence, livelihood and conduct are required, with limited exceptions to releasing another citizenship.
topics.scope: Selected adult ordinary naturalisation requirements under Article 12 of the Bulgarian Citizenship Act, as published through June 2026; descent, marriage-related reductions, protection and exceptional grants are separate.

facts.label: Five years since settled permission
facts.text: The ordinary applicant must be an adult and have obtained permanent or long-term residence permission at least five years before applying. This is not five years from any first visit or temporary residence permit.

constraint.cohort: Article 12 ordinary applicant: measured since permission for permanent OR long-term residence; not total residence since initial immigration

facts.label: Livelihood, criminal and security checks
facts.text: Income or an occupation must support the applicant in Bulgaria. Bulgarian convictions or pending proceedings for intentional public-prosecution offences can disqualify, subject to rehabilitation. Serious public-order, public-morality, public-health or national-security concerns require refusal even where other conditions are met.
facts.locator: Article 12(1)(3)-(4) and Article 19

facts.label: Release rule and nationality exceptions
facts.text: Release from the previous citizenship is normally required, or must occur upon Bulgarian acquisition. Exceptions include spouses of Bulgarian citizens, EU/EEA/Swiss citizens and citizens of countries covered by a reciprocal treaty. Another country's retention rules still need checking.
facts.locator: Article 12(1)(6) and 12(2)

facts.label: Education or citizenship-language evidence
facts.text: Specified Bulgarian school or higher-education documents can establish language knowledge; other applicants use the Ministry-regulated certification process. The published written exam has 20 questions in 60 minutes, requiring 12 correct answers. The regulation provides an oral alternative for blind applicants, specified disability groups and those over 70.
facts.locator: Ordinance 5 Articles 2-6; September 2026 examination notice on format and pass threshold

facts.label: No verified CEFR equivalence
facts.text: The regulation describes elementary normal communication, and the exam notice states a question-based pass score. Neither reviewed source maps that requirement to a CEFR level. No A1, A2 or B1 equivalent is asserted.
facts.locator: Ordinance 5 Article 6(2); examination notice, assessment criteria

facts.label: Personal filing, interview and decree
facts.text: The application is filed personally with the Justice Ministry or a Bulgarian diplomatic or consular representation, with an interview. Naturalisation is effected by a presidential decree taking effect when issued; satisfying residence alone does not confer citizenship.
facts.locator: Articles 29(1)-(3) and 36

limits: Some family, birthplace, descent and protection cohorts qualify under different provisions. No five-year total immigration-to-citizenship guarantee or ordinary investment shortcut is inferred.
The residence constraint includes long-term residence permission as expressly stated in its qualification; it must not be displayed as a permanent-residence-only rule.

The language regulation's displayed consolidation is through 2015, and it remains linked by the official September 2026 exam notice. Disability, overseas examination and education-proof arrangements require the applicable procedure, not a universal written-test assumption.

topics.title: Bulgaria Tax Residence and Foreign Income
topics.summary: Bulgarian tax residence is determined independently of nationality through address, presence, vital interests and specified overseas assignments. It normally changes the income-tax scope from Bulgarian sources to worldwide income.
topics.scope: Selected individual residence and income-scope rules from current NRA guidance, corroborated against its Act consolidation through March 2026; not an annual-rate calculation, corporate-tax guide or individual treaty opinion.

facts.label: Residence tests do not depend on citizenship
facts.text: Domestic tests include a Bulgarian permanent address, presence exceeding 183 days in any twelve-month period, a Bulgarian centre of vital interests, or specified assignments abroad by Bulgarian state bodies or enterprises and accompanying family. The permanent-address rule has an important foreign-vital-interests exception.
facts.locator: NRA resident definition; Personal Income Tax Act Article 4(1), (5)

facts.label: Strictly more than 183 days
facts.text: The presence test applies to the year in which the 183-day threshold is exceeded. Entry and exit days count as days of presence. Stays exclusively for study or medical treatment are excluded from this test, not necessarily from the other residence tests.
facts.locator: NRA presence-counting paragraphs; Article 4(2)-(3)

facts.label: A Bulgarian address is not conclusive
facts.text: A person with a Bulgarian permanent address but a centre of vital interests outside Bulgaria is not resident under the stated exception. Family, property, work or business activity and where property is managed are relevant to locating those interests.
facts.locator: NRA centre-of-vital-interests explanation; Article 4(4)-(5)

facts.label: Worldwide residents; Bulgarian-source non-residents
facts.text: Residents generally face tax on domestic and foreign income; non-residents on Bulgarian-source income. Work or services performed in Bulgaria and income from Bulgarian real estate are source examples. The place where payment is received does not determine source by itself. Exemptions and treaties still apply.
facts.locator: NRA obligations and Bulgarian-source sections; Articles 6-8, especially 8(2), (10), (12)

facts.label: Double-tax relief depends on the treaty
facts.text: Depending on the applicable treaty, relief may use foreign-tax credit or exemption with progression. The NRA identifies dedicated annual-return schedules for these methods. This does not establish that every income item must be declared or that foreign tax is always fully refunded.
facts.locator: NRA section on methods for eliminating double taxation and annual-return schedules

limits: A Bulgarian passport does not itself prove tax residence or exempt overseas income. Treaty residence, the particular income category and statutory exemptions need individual review.

The Act file is served as DOCX despite its .rtf URL and is expressly identified by its March 2026 consolidation date. These selected rules are also stated on the currently accessible NRA guidance pages; no claim is made that the download contains every later amendment.

Rates, allowances, social insurance, special business regimes and filing calculations are outside this baseline. The source page's shortened description of days during a year is not used to replace Article 4's any-twelve-month-period rule.
